questions.q: What is the core difference between authentication and authorization?
options: They are two names for the exact same process
Authentication establishes who a user is; authorization determines what that authenticated user is allowed to do
Authorization always happens before authentication
Authentication only applies to external systems, never to Salesforce itself
questions.explain: A user can be authenticated perfectly (we're certain who they are) while still being authorized for very little, or the reverse — keeping the two questions conceptually separate is central to sound identity architecture.

questions.q: In a single sign-on setup where Salesforce trusts an external corporate directory to authenticate users, what role is Salesforce playing?
options: Identity provider
Service provider
Neither role; Salesforce is unaffected by SSO configuration
Both roles simultaneously in every SSO configuration
questions.explain: When Salesforce trusts an external system's login instead of authenticating the user itself, Salesforce is acting as the service provider, trusting the identity provider's vouching for who the user is.

questions.q: During a SAML-based login, what does the identity provider send to the service provider after checking its own records?
options: The user's actual password in plain text
A signed assertion confirming the user's identity, which the service provider verifies before trusting it
Nothing; the service provider authenticates the user independently
A request asking the user to re-enter their credentials a second time
questions.explain: The identity provider returns a signed assertion vouching for the user's identity; the service provider verifies that signature before trusting it and granting access — all happening in the background during login.

questions.q: What does a Federation ID actually do in a Salesforce SSO setup?
options: It links a Salesforce user record to that user's identity on the external identity provider's side, and must be unique per user in the org
It replaces the need for a profile or permission set entirely
It is a global setting that applies to every Salesforce org simultaneously
It encrypts data at rest for the user's records
questions.explain: The Federation ID is the shared identifier that lets a service provider know which of its own user records corresponds to the identity an identity provider just vouched for — it must be unique per user within the org, and email is a common choice for it.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say an identity decision rarely stays contained to identity alone?
options: Because identity decisions have no real consequences outside their own domain

Because federating authentication raises security questions (does access follow deprovisioning), integration questions (monitoring the IdP connection), and development-lifecycle questions (safe testing) all at once
Because Salesforce forbids identity decisions from affecting security settings
Because only development teams are affected by identity decisions, never security or integration teams
questions.explain: Choosing to federate authentication through a corporate identity provider immediately raises questions in security (deprovisioning), integration (the IdP connection itself), and development lifecycle (safe sandbox testing) — the same cross-domain pattern Lesson 4 introduced.
